title: God or mammon
source_text: Κἂν τῷ ἑαυτοῦ οὖν λόγῳ πασσυδὶ ἡμᾶς ἀποπέμπῃ τοῦ βίου ὁ Κέλσος, ἵν᾿, ὡς νομίζει, ἐρημωθῇ πάμπαν ἐπὶ γῆς τὸ τοιοῦτον ἡμῶν γένος, ἀλλ᾿ ἡμεῖς ἐν τοῖς τοῦ κτίσαντος ἡμᾶς κατὰ τοὺς τοῦ θεοῦ βιώσομεν νόμους, οὐδαμῶς δουλεύειν θέλοντες τοῖς τῆς ἁμαρτίας νόμοις. καὶ γυναῖκας. ἐὰν βουλώμεθα, ἀξόμεθα καὶ παῖδας διδομένους ἡμῖν ἐν τοῖς γάμοις ἡμῶν ληψόμεθα. ἐὰν δὲ δέῃ, καὶ τῶν ἐν τῷ βίῳ μεθέξομεν, ἀνεχόμενοι τῶν ἐπιτεταγμένων κακῶν· ὡς πειρασμῶν τῆς ψυχῆς. οὕτως γὰρ ἔθος τοῖς θείοις ὀνομάζειν λόγοις τὰ συμβαίνοντα ἐν ἀνθρώποις· ἐν οἷς ὡς χρυσὸς ἐν πυρὶ ἡ τοῦ ἀνθρώπου βασανιζομένη ψυχὴ ἤτοι ἐλέγχεται ἢ θαυμαστὴ εἶναι ἀναφαίνεται. καὶ οὕτως γε πρὸς ἃ λέγει κακὰ Κέλσος παρεσκευάσμεθα, ὥστε καὶ λέγειν ἡμᾶς· „δοκίμασόν με. κύριε, καὶ πείρασόν με, πύρωσον τοὺς νεφρούς μου καὶ τὴν καρδίαν μου.“ καὶ γὰρ οὐδεὶς „στεφανοῦται, ἐὰν μὴ νομίμως“ ἐνταῦθα καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς μετὰ σώματος τοῦ „τῆς ταπεινώσεως“ „ἀθλήσῃ.“ πρὸς δὲ τούτοις οὐδὲ ἀποδίδομεν τὰς νομιζομένας προσήκειν τιμὰς οἷς λέγει Κέλσος τὰ τῇδε ἐπιτετράφθαι. „κύριον“ γὰρ „τὸν θεὸν“ ἡμῶν προσκυνοῦμεν „καὶ αὐτῷ μόνῳ“ λατρεύομεν, εὐχόμενοι μιμηταὶ Χριστοῦ γίνεσθαι. ὃς τῷ εἰπόντι αὐτῷ διαβόλῳ· „ταῦτά σοι πάντα δώσω, ἐὰν πεσὼν προσκυνήσῃς μοι“ εἶπε τό· „κύριον τὸν θεόν σου προσκυνήσεις καὶ αὐτῷ μόνῳ λατρεύσεις.“ καὶ διὸ τοῦτό γε τὰς νομιζομένας προσήκειν τιμὰς οἷς φησι Κέλσος τὰ τῇδε ἐπιτετράφθαι οὐκ ἀποδίδομεν, ἐπεὶ „οὐδεὶς δύναται δυσὶ κυρίοις δουλεύειν“ καὶ οὐ δυνάμεθα ἅμα „θεῷ δουλεύειν καὶ μαμωνᾷ,“ εἴθ᾿ ὅ τι ποτὲ ἓν ἢ πλείονα καλουμένῳ. ἀλλὰ καὶ εἰ „διὰ τῆς παραβάσεως τοῦ νόμου“ ἀτιμάζει τις τὸν νομοθετοῦντα, σαφὲς ἡμῖν φαίνεται ὅτι δύο νόμων ἐναντιότητα πρὸς ἀλλήλους ἐχόντων. τοῦ νόμου τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τοῦ νόμου τοῦ μαμωνᾶ. αἱρετώτερον ἡμᾶς „διὰ τῆς παραβάσεως τοῦ νόμου“ τοῦ μαμωνᾶ τὸν μαμωνᾶν ἀτιμάζειν, ἵνα διὰ τῆς τηρήσεως τοῦ νόμου τοῦ θεοῦ τὸν θεὸν τιμήσωμεν, ἢ „διὰ τῆς παραβάσεως τοῦ νόμου“ τοῦ θεοῦ τὸν θεὸν ἀτιμάζειν, ἵνα τηρήσει τοῦ νόμου τοῦ μαμωνᾶ τὸν μαμωνᾶν τιμήσωμεν.
pass_a_gloss: Even if, then, by his own argument (λόγος) Celsus sends us away (ἀποπέμπω) from life all together (πασσυδί), so that, as he thinks (νομίζω), such a race (γένος) of ours be made desolate (ἐρημόω) altogether upon earth, yet we in the things of him who created (κτίζω) us shall live (βιόω) according to the laws (νόμος) of God, in no way wishing to be slaves (δουλεύω) to the laws of sin (ἁμαρτία). And wives, if we wish (βούλομαι), we shall take, and children given to us in our marriages (γάμος) we shall receive (λαμβάνω). And if need be (δέῃ), we shall partake of the things in life, enduring (ἀνέχομαι) the appointed (ἐπιτάσσω) evils as trials (πειρασμός) of the soul. For so the divine words (θεῖοι λόγοι) are accustomed (ἔθος) to name the things befalling (συμβαίνω) among men; in which, as gold (χρυσός) in fire (πῦρ), the soul of man being tested (βασανίζω) is either convicted/exposed (ἐλέγχω) or appears (ἀναφαίνομαι) to be admirable (θαυμαστός). And so we are prepared (παρασκευάζω) for what Celsus calls evils, that we even say: 'test (δοκιμάζω) me, Lord, and try (πειράζω) me, burn/refine (πυρόω) my kidneys (νεφροί) and my heart (καρδία).' For no one is crowned (στεφανόω) unless he competes (ἀθλέω) lawfully (νομίμως) here and on earth with the body of humiliation (ταπείνωσις). Besides these, we do not render (ἀποδίδωμι) the honours (τιμή) thought fitting (προσήκω) to those to whom Celsus says things here have been entrusted (ἐπιτρέπω). For the Lord our God we worship (προσκυνέω) and to him alone we serve/worship (λατρεύω), praying (εὔχομαι) to become imitators (μιμητής) of Christ; who to the devil saying to him, 'all these I will give you, if falling down (πίπτω) you worship me', said: 'the Lord your God you shall worship and him alone you shall serve.' And for this reason we do not render the honours thought fitting to those to whom Celsus says things here are entrusted, since no one can be slave (δουλεύω) to two lords (κύριος), and we cannot at the same time (ἅμα) be slaves to God and mammon (μαμωνᾶς), whether whatever one or more is so called. But also, if through the transgression (παράβασις) of the law someone dishonours (ἀτιμάζω) the lawgiver (νομοθετέω), it appears clear to us that, two laws having opposition (ἐναντιότης) to one another, the law of God and the law of mammon, it is more choiceworthy (αἱρετώτερον) for us through transgression of the law of mammon to dishonour mammon, so that through keeping (τήρησις) of the law of God we may honour (τιμάω) God, than through transgression of the law of God to dishonour God, so that by keeping the law of mammon we may honour mammon.
pass_b_english: So even if, by his own argument, Celsus sends us one and all out of life, so that, as he thinks, such a race of ours may be wholly wiped out from the earth, we for our part will live among the works of the One who created us, according to the laws of God, in no way willing to be slaves to the laws of sin (Romans 7:25). And we will marry, if we wish, and receive the children given to us in our marriages. And if need be, we will share in the things of life, bearing the appointed evils as trials of the soul. For this is what the divine words usually call what befalls men; and in these the soul of man, tested like gold in the fire, is either exposed or shown to be admirable (1 Peter 1:6–7; Sirach 2:5).

And we are so prepared for what Celsus calls evils that we even say, “Test me, Lord, and try me; put my inmost parts and my heart to the fire” (Psalm 26:2). For no one “is crowned unless he competes according to the rules” (2 Timothy 2:5) here on earth, with “the body of humiliation” (Philippians 3:21).

Moreover, we do not render the honours thought to be due to those to whom, Celsus says, the things here have been entrusted. For we worship “the Lord” our “God” and serve “him alone” (Matthew 4:10), praying to become imitators of Christ (1 Corinthians 11:1). When the devil said to him, “All these things I will give you, if you will fall down and worship me” (Matthew 4:9), he answered, “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matthew 4:10). That is why we do not render the honours thought fitting to those to whom, Celsus says, the things here have been entrusted: because “no one can serve two masters” (Matthew 6:24), and we cannot at once “serve God and mammon” (Matthew 6:24), whether that name belongs to one being or to many.

Further, if anyone dishonours the lawgiver “through transgression of the law” (Romans 2:23), it seems clear to us that, when two laws stand opposed to each other, the law of God and the law of mammon, it is better for us to dishonour mammon “through transgression of the law” of mammon, so that by keeping the law of God we may honour God, than to dishonour God “through transgression of the law” of God, so that by keeping the law of mammon we may honour mammon.

choices.choice: Origen answers Celsus’s words in 8.55 point by point (πασσυδί, ἐρημωθῇ πάμπαν, take wives, children, share in life, appointed evils, render honours, those entrusted); the English keeps the same wording in both chapters. ἐν τοῖς τοῦ κτίσαντος ἡμᾶς has no expressed noun; ‘among the works of’ supplies it. ‘Slaves to the laws of sin’ alludes to Romans 7:25 (also 7:23), where the law of sin is singular. ‘Tested like gold in the fire’ with πειρασμοί (‘trials’) matches 1 Peter 1:6–7; ‘we are prepared’ and ‘gold is tested in fire’ also echo Sirach 2:1, 5; both cited. Psalm 26:2 = LXX Psalm 25:2, wording identical; νεφροί (‘kidneys’, the seat of the inner self) rendered ‘inmost parts’. 2 Timothy 2:5: νομίμως ἀθλήσῃ, ‘competes according to the rules’; Origen inserts ἐνταῦθα καὶ ἐπὶ γῆς μετὰ σώματος τοῦ τῆς ταπεινώσεως inside the verse, and the English places ‘here on earth, with the body of humiliation’ after the quotation. Philippians 3:21 ‘body of humiliation’ as in 8.54. Matthew 4:10 itself quotes Deuteronomy 6:13 (also Luke 4:8); Origen frames it as Christ’s reply, so Matthew is cited; ‘the Lord our God’ in the first use is Origen’s adaptation. ‘Imitators of Christ’ alludes to 1 Corinthians 11:1. ‘Whether that name belongs to one being or to many’ renders εἴθ᾿ ὅ τι ποτὲ ἓν ἢ πλείονα καλουμένῳ, a hint that ‘mammon’ may name a demon or demons. Romans 2:23 (διὰ τῆς παραβάσεως τοῦ νόμου τὸν θεὸν ἀτιμάζεις) is repeated three times by Origen; cited once at the first use.
'For so the divine words are accustomed to name' (stiff) -> 'For this is what the divine words usually call'
πρὸς ἃ λέγει κακὰ: 'prepared against' -> 'prepared for'
μετὰ σώματος: 'in the body "of humiliation"' -> 'with "the body of humiliation"'; stray comma before 'here on earth' removed
All eleven references checked against the verse; LXX Psalm 25:2 -> Psalm 26:2 confirmed
